channel.title: The Pointe at Kirby Gate: Senior Living News
channel.description: Senior housing, senior care and caregiving news from trusted publishers, gathered every day by our team. The summaries are ours; the full stories belong to their publishers.

item.title: Senior housing occupancy nears a record high as most major markets pass 90%
item.description: New third-quarter data from NIC MAP shows senior housing occupancy across the largest U.S. markets rose to about 90.4%, close to a record. Assisted living saw the biggest gain of any housing type, climbing to about 89.1%, while independent living reached about 91.7%. More than half of the primary markets NIC tracks are now above 90% full. At the same time, new construction remains near historic lows, so the supply of new apartments is growing very slowly. Why it matters: With communities filling up and little new construction, families who start looking early tend to have more choices.

item.title: Family caregivers' out-of-pocket costs up about 60% in five years, AARP study finds
item.description: New AARP research reported by NPR finds that family caregivers now spend an average of about $11,508 a year of their own money on caregiving, roughly 60% more than five years ago. That amounts to around 31% of a typical caregiver's income, and the share is far higher for lower-income households. The story frames the cost of caregiving as rising even faster than rent or gas, putting pressure on family budgets and retirement savings. Why it matters: Caring for a parent at home has real costs that are easy to underestimate; a benefits counselor can help a family look at the full picture.

item.title: AARP: 12 ways family caregivers can get through their hardest days
item.description: AARP collects a dozen practical strategies for family caregivers on days when patience runs thin. The guide covers handling anger when a loved one falls, wanders or makes a mess, including letting frustration out away from the person rather than in front of them. It also addresses dealing with paperwork and bureaucracy, setting boundaries, and making time for interests that caregivers often give up. The advice draws on caregiving researchers, including a Stanford expert on family caregiver stress. Why it matters: Hard days are a normal part of caring for a parent, and having a few strategies ready can make them easier to get through.

item.title: Guides & Resources: our new library of guides for families
item.description: We have opened Guides & Resources, a library of plain-language guides for families comparing assisted living and memory care in East Memphis, written by the people who answer these questions every day. The first guide, Questions to Ask on an Assisted Living Tour, covers what to ask about care, staffing, daily life, cost and contracts, and what to notice while you are in the building. More guides are on the way. Why it matters: a tour is the one part of this decision you can do in person, and the right questions make it count.

item.title: Assisted living costs rose about 5 percent in 2025, CareScout survey finds
item.description: CareScout's annual Cost of Care Survey, drawn from roughly 16,000 responses from long-term care providers across the country, found that the national median cost of an assisted living community rose about 5 percent in 2025. Home care and nursing home rates rose as well, and a private nursing home room still runs roughly three-quarters more than assisted living. The report breaks the medians down by state and by type of care. Why it matters: rates vary a great deal from one community to the next, so ask exactly what a monthly rate includes before you compare.

item.title: 7.4 million older Americans are living with Alzheimer's, new report finds
item.description: The Alzheimer's Association's 2026 Facts and Figures report estimates that 7.4 million Americans age 65 and older are living with Alzheimer's, and that more than 12 million family members and friends provided unpaid care last year, most of them describing the emotional strain as high. A companion survey found that nearly everyone values brain health, yet fewer than one in ten feel they know much about protecting it. Why it matters: the report lists everyday habits linked to lower risk, such as staying active, sleeping well and managing blood pressure, which makes a good conversation to have with a parent's doctor.

item.title: Walk to End Alzheimer's returns to Shelby Farms Park on November 7
item.description: The Alzheimer's Association's Memphis Walk to End Alzheimer's takes place on Saturday, November 7, 2026, at Shelby Farms Park. On-site registration opens at 8 a.m. and the Promise Garden ceremony, where walkers carry flowers that stand for their connection to the disease, begins at 9 a.m. Individuals and teams from across the Mid-South take part, and the money raised supports care, support programs and research. Why it matters: It is a welcoming way for families touched by dementia to meet others in the same place.

item.title: More years of school linked to lower dementia risk decades later, study finds
item.description: A USC-led study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences used a 1972 British policy that raised the school-leaving age as a natural experiment. People who stayed in school longer because of that change were less likely to be diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease and related dementias decades later. The researchers report that the benefit held even among people with a high genetic risk of the disease. Why it matters: It adds to research on dementia risk factors that can change over a lifetime; a doctor can talk through brain health with your parent.

item.title: Medicare open enrollment is underway: what changes in 2027
item.description: Medicare's yearly open enrollment runs from October 15 through December 7, 2026, and any change made in that window takes effect on January 1. Among the shifts arriving in 2027 are a higher yearly cap on out-of-pocket drug costs in Part D, the end of a temporary program that had held down some standalone drug plan premiums, and new negotiated prices for 15 more high-cost medicines. Some Medicare Advantage plans are also leaving certain areas or trimming benefits, so the plan's annual notice of change is worth reading closely. Why it matters: If a parent's plan or medicines are changing, a free Medicare counselor (SHIP) can help compare options before December 7.
